title: Events and the transactional outbox
summary: Follow one saved note and its notification to understand why two separate writes can disagree, and how an outbox makes the work recoverable.
objectives: Distinguish a request to do work from a fact that already happened.
Trace the two-write failure that an outbox addresses.
Explain why consumers still need duplicate-safe behavior.

terms.definition: A record of a fact that happened, such as NotePublished, with an identity and relevant data.
Updating two separate systems as part of one logical action without a shared atomic commit.
An outgoing-work record saved in the same database transaction as the business change.
A worker that reads committed outbox entries and publishes them to another system.
Repeating an operation with the same identity does not repeat its intended business effect.

retrieval: Why can a worker receive a queue message more than once?
What does committing a database transaction make atomic?

sections.title: A saved note should produce an activity update
sections.markdown:
Pocket Notes can now publish a note to a small shared workspace. Saving the publication is essential. Updating a team activity page can happen shortly afterward. We could make the request handler save the note and then send a message saying “this note was published.”

The message describes a past fact, so we call it an event: NotePublished. By contrast, PublishNote is a command asking the application to attempt an action. The command can fail validation or permission checks; the event should represent something that actually committed.

An event might carry eventId, noteId, workspaceId, noteVersion, and publishedAt. Include the information a legitimate consumer needs, while avoiding unnecessary private note text. A timestamp helps observation but does not by itself establish a reliable global order across computers.

sections.title: Two successful writes are not one atomic action
sections.markdown:
The app must save a publication and arrange its activity update. A reliable database plus a reliable broker does not make two separate calls one atomic action.

| Order of calls | Crash or failure between them | Incorrect outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commit note, then send event | Process stops before sending | Published note with no recorded activity obligation |
| Send event, then commit note | Database transaction fails | Event announces a publication that never committed |

Retrying the whole request is not a complete answer. The caller may never retry, and a retry may repeat work that already succeeded.

The missing concept is a **durable obligation**: a record that downstream work remains owed. Earlier transactions protected related rows inside one database. Put the publication fact and its outgoing obligation inside that boundary, rather than pretending an asynchronous arrow commits both stores.

sections.title: Save the fact and its outgoing work together
sections.markdown:
In one database transaction, publish the note and insert an outbox row. The outbox is a table of outgoing events still owed to downstream systems.

~~~text
BEGIN
  note n28: status = published, version = 6
  outbox E28: type = NotePublished, noteId = n28, version = 6
COMMIT
~~~

Either both rows commit or neither does. The request may return after this commit; the activity page is still allowed to lag.

| Participant | Responsibility | Durable evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request handler | Accept the business change and publication intent together | Note row plus outbox row |
| Relay | Publish committed outgoing work and track progress | Retained outbox identity/state |
| Activity consumer | Apply one accepted activity effect despite repeated events | Its own protected event/effect record |

The relay sends a row's event to the broker, then records publication progress. A crash after broker acceptance can repeat the publication; the next section handles this remaining gap.

Watch the oldest unsent row and available relay throughput. If publication stalls, obligations accumulate. Retry with limits and backoff, investigate stuck work, and keep enough data to recover. Deleting an unsent row merely to make a dashboard green discards the promise.

sections.title: The relay still has an uncertain moment
sections.markdown:
Suppose the broker accepts event E42. The relay crashes before marking its outbox row sent. After restart, the row still looks unsent, so the relay publishes E42 again. Marking it sent before publishing would create the opposite risk: a crash could lose the event. The outbox closes one atomicity gap; it does not magically remove all uncertainty.

For a database-backed activity consumer, one useful pattern is to insert E42 into a processed-events table and insert the activity entry in the same local transaction. A unique key on the event identity lets a later duplicate detect that the effect already committed. If that transaction fails, neither record should falsely claim success.

External effects need a separate contract. A processed-events row cannot atomically cover an unrelated email provider or payment service. Use a provider-supported idempotency key when available, record outcomes, and reconcile uncertain results. Do not claim “exactly once everywhere” because one local table deduplicates messages.

sections.title: Version facts and practice recovery
sections.markdown:
Two edits can create events for note versions 7 and 8. If a downstream view receives 8 then 7, blindly applying both can move it backward. For a view that stores the latest full representation, compare the version and reject older updates under a defined ordering rule. For incremental changes, skipping a missing predecessor may be unsafe; choose the event format and ordering policy deliberately.

An outbox can be relayed by polling or by reading database change records. The latter approach is called change data capture and appears again later. Either way, start with the same question: which committed business change owes which downstream work?

In an interview, draw the database transaction boundary first, then the asynchronous arrow. Explain the crash before publish and the crash after broker acceptance. A convincing answer includes both recovery and duplicates, plus a visible lag measure for users who depend on the downstream result.

diagrams.source:

H[Publish request] --> T[Database transaction]
T --> N[(Published note)]

Q --> C[Duplicate-safe activity consumer]
diagrams.caption: The note and outbox entry share a commit. Broker publication happens afterward and may repeat.
steps: Commit the note and outbox row together.
Apply each event identity safely at the consumer.

diagrams.title: The outbox fixes one gap while the relay can still repeat
diagrams.source:
sequenceDiagram
participant R as Relay
participant B as Broker
participant D as Outbox database
R->>D: Read unsent event E28
R->>B: Publish E28
B-->>R: Accepted under broker contract
Note over R: Crashes before recording progress
R->>D: Restart and read unsent E28
R->>B: Publish same E28 again
diagrams.caption: Consumer deduplication must protect its effect. This sequence does not include arbitrary external calls in the outbox database transaction.
steps: Publish it with its stable identity.
Recognize the crash after broker acceptance as an uncertain progress boundary.
Make repeated delivery harmless at the consumer’s authoritative effect.

exercise.prompt: Draw a timeline where E42 is published twice after a relay crash. Show the note row, outbox row, broker, processed-events table, and activity entry. Mark the two separate transaction boundaries.
rubric: The note and outbox commit together.
A crash after broker acceptance explains the duplicate.
Deduplication and the local activity effect commit together.
exercise.solution: Transaction one commits the published note and E42 outbox row. The relay sends E42; the broker accepts it; the relay crashes before marking the row sent. After restart it sends E42 again. The activity consumer uses transaction two to claim E42 with a unique event identity and create the activity entry. A duplicate finds the committed identity and does not create a second entry. This protects the local database effect; an external notification needs its own idempotency/reconciliation contract.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the same outbox transaction?
options: The note update and its outgoing event row
questions.answer: The note update and its outgoing event row
questions.explanation: The shared local commit prevents committed business state from losing its recorded publication obligation.

questions.prompt: Can a correct outbox relay publish the same event twice?
options: Only if the note was never committed
questions.explanation: Broker acceptance followed by a crash before the sent marker creates uncertainty and a possible retry.

options: A request that may not succeed
A committed fact about a publication
A promise that every subscriber is already updated
questions.answer: A committed fact about a publication
questions.explanation: Events describe facts; downstream processing may still be pending.

questions.prompt: Why is marking an outbox row sent before publishing unsafe?
questions.answer: A crash after the marker but before broker acceptance could permanently skip publication.
questions.explanation: A crash after the marker but before broker acceptance could permanently skip publication.

questions.prompt: Why does local event deduplication not guarantee one email?
questions.answer: The local transaction cannot also atomically commit an unrelated provider action; use supported provider idempotency and reconcile uncertain outcomes.
questions.explanation: The local transaction cannot also atomically commit an unrelated provider action; use supported provider idempotency and reconcile uncertain outcomes.

flashcards.back: One system commits while the second action is lost or inconsistent.
Business change plus outgoing-work row in one database transaction.
Acceptance may happen before the durable sent marker.
Event identity and business effect commit atomically together.
Age and size of unsent work, plus recovery throughput and errors.

mentalModel: Record what you owe in the same commit as what you changed; fulfill that obligation with retry-safe processing.

walkthroughs.title: A committed note keeps its outgoing work after a crash
walkthroughs.intro: Follow note n28 and event E28. The note row and outbox row share one database; the activity projection is separate.

steps.title: Before publication
steps.explanation: The note is a draft. There is no accepted publication event.

steps.title: Commit both facts
steps.explanation: One transaction publishes version 6 and records E28. The downstream page may still show its old state.

steps.title: Handler stops before sending
steps.explanation: A process crash does not erase the obligation because it was committed with the note.

steps.title: Relay and consumer make progress
steps.explanation: The relay publishes E28. A duplicate-tolerant consumer commits its activity effect; relay progress is recorded under its own protocol.

walkthroughs.takeaway: The outbox is saved evidence of work owed. It removes the lost-obligation gap while leaving explicit relay and consumer recovery rules.
